content: To submit a proposal to an ethics review board, it is essential to include a draft of the interview questionnaire and a detailed list of the types of data intended for collection. Consent forms must also be submitted, as they are mandatory for all staff members who will be interviewed or who will provide data to the data collector. Sample facility information sheets and consent forms are available for reference in Appendix 12. These samples can be adapted to align with local ethical guidelines and the specific context of the study. The Value TB Costing Tool Suite is designed to facilitate the collection of data and the calculation of unit costs for tuberculosis (TB) service delivery at the facility level. It supports both top-down and bottom-up costing approaches, as well as economic and financial cost methodologies. The tool accommodates various methods for measuring staff time, including interviews, observations, and timesheets, and allows for disaggregation by key input categories. However, it does not support community-based costing. For above-facility cost data collection, an additional data collection instrument, currently under development, will be required. The Value TB Costing Tool Suite has certain limitations. To maintain feasibility within a reasonable timeframe, some components of TB interventions have been excluded. For instance, unit costs for individual adverse events related to TB treatment or prevention have not been derived, nor is the list of monitoring tests for identifying these events comprehensive. However, the tool does allow for the inclusion of costs associated with inpatient care, including time spent managing adverse drug reactions from anti-TB medications. The most commonly used adverse event monitoring tests are included and can be costed. When adapting the Value TB Costing Tool Suite to a specific country context, the process involves four main steps. First, the study team defines the TB interventions to be costed during the protocol development phase. Second, the production process and potential data sources are identified, with data collectors re-evaluating these for each facility during site visits. Third, pilot testing is conducted, which may take up to two weeks if a wide range of TB interventions is selected. Following the pilot, the tool is adapted to the country context. During this adaptation, the research team should incorporate as many context-specific and country-appropriate service outputs, drug names, test procedures, service utilization labels, consumable supplies, staff titles, and department or clinic names as possible. The data analysis phase is a critical component of the costing process, requiring adequate allocation of resources, including research staff and funding. The primary goal is to use the prices and quantities collected at each facility and above-facility level to calculate total and unit costs that align with the study's objectives. However, these costs must be contextualized to provide meaningful insights into the factors driving costs. Differences can be analyzed by subgroups, such as drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). If the sample size permits, statistical differences between population or facility groups can also be examined. Descriptive analyses may include evaluating the average number of visits per patient for different patient groups or subgroups (e.g., pulmonary TB, extrapulmonary TB, new cases, and retreatment cases) and the breakdown of visit types (e.g., diagnostic visits, treatment visits, community treatment visits, inpatient bed-days). Costs per input, including mean, standard deviation, median, and interquartile range, can be assessed for different interventions and patient groups. For example, the cost of first-line treatment can be analyzed across facilities, broken down by input categories such as diagnostic tests (e.g., Xpert® MTB/RIF, microscopy), treatment visits, and inpatient bed-days. Variations within a country in the number of visits per patient by visit type and health facility level can also be explored. Additionally, the proportion of costs allocated to inputs such as personnel, building space, equipment, and consumables can be evaluated to assess efficiency variability. Econometric analyses can be conducted on larger datasets to explore technical efficiency, extrapolate costs to other settings, and identify cost determinants. Sensitivity analyses are essential for identifying potential biases and uncertainties in unit cost estimates. These analyses may involve altering variables such as medication costs, utilization rates, or salary costs to assess their impact on cost estimates. Scenario analyses can help evaluate different future approaches or options. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) can be used to examine uncertainty ranges by assigning probability distributions to input data. When presenting results, it is important to tailor the presentation to the audience. Simple graphical representations, such as bar graphs, are effective for comparing costs across sites and visually highlighting the highest and lowest cost components. For policymakers, data should be presented transparently and in an easily digestible format to facilitate resource allocation decisions. For healthcare workers, the information should be translated into practical knowledge applicable to their work settings. Limitations of the study, such as interventions not costed, insufficient sample sizes, or unassessed above-facility costs, should be clearly identified and described. The generalizability and applicability of the findings should also be explained, specifying whether they are relevant to other lowand middle-income settings or only to similar facilities within the country. Finally, it is crucial to disseminate findings to stakeholders, including clinic and laboratory managers, national TB program (NTP) members, health ministries, funders, and other interested parties. Data should be made publicly accessible whenever possible, such as through platforms like the Global Health Cost Consortium (GHCC). If published in journal articles, open access should be granted to ensure the information serves as a public good. Feedback should be shared with those involved in the cost analysis, and discussions about updating cost estimates managed by NTPs should be encouraged.
